questions.q: What is a connection in Power Automate?
options: A visual link drawn between two actions in the designer
The record that a flow may authenticate as a given identity against a given service
A type of HTTP header used only by premium connectors
A folder that stores a flow's run history
questions.explain: A connection is Power Automate's record of which identity a flow authenticates as when it talks to a particular connector or service.

questions.q: Why is a user-delegated connection risky for an enterprise flow that the whole company depends on?
options: User-delegated connections cannot call any connector except SharePoint
It runs as a specific person's identity, so the flow can break if that person leaves or changes their password
User-delegated connections expire after exactly one run
They require a separate license for every flow
questions.explain: A user-delegated connection inherits one specific person's access. If that person's account changes or they leave the company, the flow's authentication can break.

options: A senior employee who approves all flow deployments
A non-human application identity in Microsoft Entra ID, authenticated with a client ID and secret instead of a password
A setting that disables authentication entirely
The main administrator account for a Power Automate environment
questions.explain: A service principal is an application identity, not a person. It authenticates with a client ID and a secret or certificate, has no mailbox, and can't log in interactively.

questions.q: Why would Castlebridge Logistics use a service principal for a flow that calls its own internal backend?
options: Because service principals are the only identity type that can call an HTTP action
Because the flow is service-to-service, not tied to a person, and shouldn't depend on any one employee's password or MFA
Because service principals are free while user accounts cost money
Because Microsoft requires it for any flow with more than five actions
questions.explain: A service-to-service call has no person behind it conceptually, so a service principal — which doesn't depend on an individual's credentials — is the appropriate identity.

questions.q: What happens in the OAuth client credentials grant that a service principal uses?
options: A user is redirected to a login page and enters their password
The flow presents its own client ID and client secret directly to the token endpoint and receives an access token, with no human involved
The flow emails an administrator to approve each request individually
Nothing — client credentials grant is only a theoretical concept, not something Power Automate actually uses
questions.explain: In the client credentials grant, the application itself (not a user) authenticates with its client ID and secret and receives a token back — there's no interactive sign-in step.
